Little Mouse’s Encyclopedia is a calm, imaginative, and beautifully illustrated interactive journey through nature, created by Circus Atos as a blend of storybook charm and educational exploration. Rather than aiming for traditional gameplay with objectives, challenges, or progression systems, it instead invites players—especially young children and families—to wander through serene habitats while learning about the animals and plants that inhabit them. The experience is gentle from the very first moment: you guide a tiny mouse through four interconnected biomes, each depicted in a richly hand-drawn style reminiscent of classic children’s picture books. The game’s foundation rests on curiosity and discovery, making it an inviting digital space for early learners or anyone who enjoys relaxing, visually expressive environments.

The art direction plays a central role in shaping the game’s identity. Every scene feels like a meticulously crafted illustration, filled with soft colors, playful character designs, and subtle animations that breathe life into each setting. Forests sway with light breeze, ponds ripple softly, and garden insects crawl or flutter in small, charming loops. These touches create a world that feels warm and comforting, even before you engage with any of its educational elements. The style is deliberately simple, but it is consistently expressive, giving the mouse—and every creature you meet—personality through visual storytelling alone. The soundscape reinforces this tone, offering quiet background music and natural ambient noises that never overwhelm the viewer but instead help settle them into a peaceful rhythm.

Interaction in Little Mouse’s Encyclopedia is intentionally minimal and intuitive. You move the mouse through sprawling but manageable scenes, and when you approach a plant or animal, a prompt allows you to learn more. The information cards are illustrated entries that present a small description of the organism, including basic facts about diet, habitat, and behavior. Each entry also includes an animation for the creature, offering a tactile sense of presence—frogs hop, beetles crawl, birds shake their wings. This combination of text and animation transforms each discovery into a miniature learning moment. The simple control scheme, along with the option to play in a wide range of languages, makes the game welcoming for very young children and accessible to families of many backgrounds.

The educational value is clear in every aspect of the experience. With over 160 species to encounter, the game provides a broad overview of wildlife and plant life across familiar natural settings. Rather than overwhelming players with deep scientific terminology, the descriptions remain approachable and age-appropriate, focusing on recognizable characteristics and foundational knowledge. The game encourages learning through immersion rather than instruction; children are free to explore at their own pace, revisit favorite areas, and linger on creatures that spark their interest. It is particularly well suited for joint play between children and parents, where conversations can naturally grow from the on-screen discoveries. As a result, it functions not just as a game, but as a digital tool for environmental curiosity and early scientific engagement.

However, the strengths of Little Mouse’s Encyclopedia also point to its limitations. The game does not offer goals, puzzles, progression systems, or problem-solving challenges, which means players looking for more structured gameplay will likely find it too passive. Because all information is accessible from the start, there is no sense of unlocking content or achieving milestones. This design choice supports free exploration, but it also means replay value relies entirely on the viewer’s interest in revisiting scenes rather than on mechanical depth. Older children or adults seeking more detailed biological information may find the entries too brief or simplistic, and some may wish for more interactive elements beyond animation and reading. The experience is also fairly short if approached as a one-time tour, though it remains engaging as a repeated activity for very young players.

Despite these limitations, Little Mouse’s Encyclopedia excels in what it sets out to do. It provides a gentle, whimsical space for learning about nature in a format that is safe, warm, and visually memorable. Its hand-drawn aesthetic is uniquely inviting, and its focus on observation over challenge makes it an ideal introduction to the natural world for children just beginning to explore wildlife and environments. For families, educators, or anyone who values quiet, curiosity-driven digital experiences, it offers something rare: a calming, screen-based activity that encourages connection with the natural world rather than fast-paced stimulation.

In the end, Little Mouse’s Encyclopedia is less a traditional videogame and more a beautifully crafted interactive nature book. Its charm, accessibility, and educational focus make it a lovely choice for young learners, while its serene presentation ensures it remains comforting and pleasant for accompanying adults. Players seeking deeper mechanics or narrative will find it limited, but for its intended audience and purpose, it stands as a thoughtful and delightful exploration of the small wonders that fill our forests, ponds, and gardens.

👁️ I'll start by saying the game absolutely deserves a thumbs-up and a recommendation. However, I’d primarily recommend it for younger children, up to pre-teens. For teenagers and adults, there’s not much to engage with — unless you're planning to use the game as an educational tool for your little ones. Personally, I picked it up to get acquainted with the genre of interactive educational games for kids.

🔍 To briefly summarize the gameplay — it’s a simple platformer where you explore locations without any enemies but with lots of interactive objects to examine. Almost every object has a short description — essentially making it a game-encyclopedia hybrid.

🐈 The game covers four biomes: field, forest, pond, and garden. In each of them, you’ll encounter typical representatives of local flora and fauna. It’s worth mentioning that the game doesn’t offer a comprehensive list of species — only a small selection is presented, which might be seen as a downside. On the plus side, nearly every element is animated and features clickable animations, which preschoolers will really enjoy.

[h3]Helpful for Steam Deck users[/h3]
🕹️ The game runs smoothly, but the device noticeably heats up.

[h3]Comments for the developers[/h3]
👷 While I have a generally positive impression, there are a few things that I believe could use some attention and polish.
[list]
[*]📗 Information cards. While flipping through them, I found most of the content was quickly forgotten and didn’t really stick. Maybe it’s just me, but I’d suggest adding a quiz mode. I’ve seen this in other educational games, and the target audience really enjoys those mechanics.
[*]📄 Text overflow issues. In a few cards, the text spills out of the box. Adding scroll functionality could solve the issue and even allow for more content.
[*]⚙️ Scene optimization. I was surprised that such a visually simple game causes my Steam Deck to heat up more than Mortal Kombat X. It runs smoothly with no bugs, but the thermal load is concerning. Might be worth reviewing how the scenes or objects are optimized.
[*]🏆 Achievements. The “discover all cards” achievement only works if you don’t exit the game. After restarting, the progress resets. Not a dealbreaker, but a bit frustrating.
[/list]

✨ The idea of creating an encyclopedia in the form of a game is fantastic. In my opinion, it's wonderful when a game can be fun, informative, and educational at the same time — a true win-win. I won’t claim the card content is life-changing, but from personal experience, you never know when some random fact about nature might come in handy. Special thanks to the developers for including Ukrainian localization — that was one of the main reasons I picked up this game.

🤗 Thanks for reading! Feel free to drop a comment if you’ve got thoughts 👇

[h3]About the Game;[/h3]
Little Mouse's Encyclopedia is a game to discover the fascinating world of nature together with Little Mouse! Together you will learn more about countless animal and plant species in their natural habitat.
All of this in beautifully painted forests, ponds and gardens, the art of the game is very nice and peaceful.
Through the different habitats/maps you can discover more than 160 animal and plant species.

Obviously it is no storyteller game, nor is it a game of difficulty.
The main target is a younger audience, to learn them about the nature around them, mainly focused on Europa.
It is a point and click style game, but the Little Mouse walks through each habitat, giving information about the animals and/or plants around you.

A Enciclopédia da Ratinha é um jogo que se destaca por sua abordagem educacional e narrativa envolvente. O jogo é centrado em uma pequena ratinha que explora o mundo ao seu redor, aprendendo e coletando informações sobre diversos tópicos, como biologia, geografia e história.

O aspecto mais cativante do jogo é a sua capacidade de ensinar de maneira lúdica. As ilustrações são encantadoras e os personagens são bem construídos, o que mantém o interesse tanto de crianças quanto de adultos. A jogabilidade é intuitiva, permitindo que os jogadores avancem de forma orgânica enquanto descobrem novos conhecimentos.

Outro ponto forte é a forma como o jogo incentiva a curiosidade e a exploração. Em vez de simplesmente apresentar fatos, ele desafia os jogadores a buscar e descobrir informações, o que torna o aprendizado mais ativo e engajador.

Em termos de melhoria, talvez a inclusão de mais desafios interativos poderia aumentar ainda mais a imersão e o engajamento dos jogadores. Além disso, uma maior diversidade de tópicos e níveis de dificuldade ajudaria a manter o interesse a longo prazo.

Em suma, "A Enciclopédia da Ratinha" é uma excelente ferramenta educacional disfarçada de jogo divertido. Ele consegue combinar aprendizado e entretenimento de forma eficaz, tornando-o uma escolha excelente para quem busca um jogo educativo de alta qualidade. Ótimo para crianças e adultos também!

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... --- TL;DR ---
I was on the fence on how to rate this. 

As a concept, it's a thumbs up. The art style is very charming and the music is nice. I think small children would enjoy interacting with the different animals, and the sound effects are subtle enough to not drive parents up the wall. It's super wholesome, and I think this is definitely a cuter and more ethical alternative to a lot of "kids games" that rely on flashing colors and micro transactions. 

But honestly, get it on iPad. This game was not designed for PC, and there are a number of game play bugs and quirks that would probably be solved by being on a touch screen. But since I'm reviewing this on steam rather than an app store, it's ultimately a thumbs down.

--- More thoughts if you want 'em ---
I have a couple gripes which I'll summarize below, but I just want to stress that it's still a great concept, and I don't think small children would notice or care about a lot of these critiques. This is mostly from the perspective of an adult who fell in love with the aesthetics and thought it would be a cute game to just zone out and explore.

The Controls:
The tutorial very clearly says you can move around the world by tapping where you want to go, or by using the arrow keys. For the life of me, I could not figure out how to move with the arrows. I tried the actual arrows, WASD, restarting the game, and it just wouldn't work. There's also an encyclopedia screen where you can go through all the entries, and the table of contents is an absolute nightmare to scroll through. It feels like it was made for touch input, and they didn't test it with a mouse. You need to scroll ages just to move a tiny bit up or down.

The Achievements:
Achievement progress within the game resets every time you quit out. So if you fully explore 2 areas in one sitting and the other 2 in a second sitting, you will get the achievements for exploring each individual area, but you will not get the achievement for exploring all the areas if that makes sense.
